Chapter 7: Forgiveness—Letting Go to Move Forward
Forgiveness—it's such a simple word, but when you’re the one who's been hurt, it can feel almost impossible, can’t it?
We all carry wounds. Some are fresh, others faded but never quite gone. And honestly, it’s tempting to hold on—to nurse that pain and wait for an apology that might never come.
But what if there’s another way? One that leads to freedom, instead of bitterness?
I’m reminded of a story about two siblings who drifted apart after a misunderstanding. Years slipped by, and the silence between them grew heavier with each passing day. Both believed the other was at fault, and pride kept them from reaching out.
Then, after hearing about a friend’s sudden loss, one sibling decided to take that scary first step. The conversation was awkward, and old hurts bubbled up almost immediately. But as they talked, something shifted. The need to be right started to fade, replaced by a real longing for connection.
Forgiveness didn’t magically erase the past, but it made room for something new to grow.
A lot of us see forgiveness as a gift for the other person. But here’s something to pay attention to—most of the time, it’s the one who forgives who’s set free.
Holding on to anger or resentment is like lugging around a heavy backpack that just gets heavier the longer you carry it. Letting go doesn’t mean you forget—or that you’re excusing what happened. It’s about choosing to release your grip on the past, and making space for healing.
There’s another memory that comes to mind—a parent, weighed down by guilt after making a mistake that hurt their child. That guilt colored every moment together, every conversation. It wasn’t until the parent spoke honestly about their regret, and the child responded with unexpected grace, that the weight finally started to lift.
Forgiveness, as it turned out, is a two-way street. It asks for vulnerability, and a bit of trust.
Most of us wait for the other person to go first—to apologize, to make things right. But here’s the hard truth: waiting almost never leads to resolution.
What if forgiveness is a choice you can make, even if the other person isn’t ready? It’s about reclaiming your power to move forward, choosing love over bitterness.
Forgiveness isn’t just a single moment, either. It’s a process—sometimes slow, sometimes uneven. There’ll be days when old pain sneaks back in, and you’ll feel that urge to hold on all over again.
But every time you choose forgiveness, the hold of the past loosens just a little more. Your heart gets lighter. And, over time, you start to see the possibility of new beginnings.
